hints: Look closely at line T. It stays at a much higher pressure than the other two lines for almost the whole 0.8 s, and it never drops down to near zero.
Remember which right-side chamber drops to very low pressure in diastole, and which vessel stays pressurised after the semilunar valve shuts to keep blood moving to the lungs.
walkthrough:
**Observe what T does**

Look at the shape first. T starts relatively high, dips a little around 0.2 s, then stays high and falls only slowly after 0.5 s. It never falls to the baseline like the other two dashed lines do.

**Recall pressures on the right side**

The right atrium and vena cava are low pressure receiving vessels, always close to zero. The right ventricle rises high during systole (about 0.2 to 0.45 s) but then must relax and fall back to near zero in diastole to allow filling.

**Spot the artery pattern**

Only a great artery stays at a higher pressure during diastole. When the ventricle relaxes, the semilunar valve closes, elastic recoil maintains pressure, and you see a small dicrotic notch around 0.45 s. That matches T perfectly, so T is the pulmonary artery on the right side.

options.A: Correct. T stays high and shows a dicrotic notch at about 0.45 s when the pulmonary semilunar valve closes, which is typical for arterial pressure.
options.B: False. Right atrial pressure is always very low with only tiny bumps during atrial systole, like one of the low dashed lines, not the high line T.
options.C: False. Right ventricular pressure rises high in systole but falls sharply to near zero in diastole, so it cannot be the line that stays high throughout.
options.D: False. Vena cava pressure is very low and follows atrial pressure closely, so it would be one of the bottom dashed lines, not the high sustained line T.
